register: wave-4 authoring register (S-B4 tranche) — part 2 of 2

items.stem: Define a diatomic molecule and list the diatomic substances named in the note.
items.modelAnswer: A diatomic molecule contains exactly two atoms; the note names H2, Cl2, O2, N2 and HCl.

items.stem: State how many shared pairs the bonds in oxygen and in nitrogen contain, and what bond name each earns.
items.modelAnswer: Oxygen shares two pairs, giving a double bond, and nitrogen shares three pairs, giving a triple bond.

items.stem: Explain why each shared pair in a dot-and-cross drawing is drawn with one electron shown as a dot and one as a cross.
items.modelAnswer: Each shared pair in the drawing uses one electron from each atom, and keeping the donor symbols visible shows exactly which atom supplied each electron of the pair.

items.stem: A student draws a dot-and-cross diagram for fluorine, F2, showing four shared electrons between the two atoms. Using the halogen bonding pattern of record, correct the drawing.
items.modelAnswer: Like the other halogens, fluorine forms a single covalent bond, so only one pair is shared in F2; the drawing should show exactly two shared electrons, one from each atom.

items.stem: Describe the bonding pattern of carbon dioxide in a dot-and-cross diagram.
items.modelAnswer: Carbon dioxide shares two pairs with each oxygen atom, making two double bonds in the molecule.

items.stem: State how many C-H single bonds methane has and what extra bond ethane adds between its carbons.
items.modelAnswer: Methane has four single C-H bonds, and ethane adds a C-C single bond between its two carbon atoms.

items.stem: Explain what the formula C2H4 tells you about the bonding between ethene's two carbon atoms.
items.modelAnswer: Ethene contains a C=C double bond: two shared pairs sit between its two carbon atoms, so the carbons are joined by two covalent bonds at once.

items.stem: A student must draw a dot-and-cross diagram for chloromethane, CH3Cl. Using the organic-molecules-in-scope rule of record, state what the diagram must contain.
items.modelAnswer: Chloromethane is in scope because organic molecules in this skill contain up to two carbon atoms, including versions with halogen atoms attached; the diagram shows four single bonds from the carbon — three C-H bonds and one C-Cl bond — with every outer electron drawn.

items.stem: Describe the arrangement of ions in an ionic solid.
items.modelAnswer: An ionic compound packs positive and negative ions alternately into a regular giant lattice.

items.stem: State how the size of the charges on ions affects the strength of the forces and the melting point.
items.modelAnswer: The larger the charges on the ions, the stronger the forces and the higher the melting point.

items.stem: Explain why so much thermal energy is needed to melt an ionic solid.
items.modelAnswer: Strong electrostatic forces of attraction between opposite charges hold the lattice together in all directions, so a large amount of thermal energy is needed to overcome them before the solid melts.

items.stem: A comparison table lists sodium chloride and magnesium oxide with their ion charges. Using the charge rule of record, predict which melts at the higher temperature and justify the prediction.
items.modelAnswer: Magnesium oxide melts at the higher temperature: its ions carry 2+ and 2- charges, larger than the single charges of sodium chloride, so its forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate them.

items.stem: State what a current needs in order to flow, in terms of particles.
items.modelAnswer: Electrical conduction needs mobile charged particles, such as electrons or ions, to carry the current.

items.stem: State what happens to the ions of an ionic compound when it dissolves in water, and what this allows.
items.modelAnswer: Dissolving in water releases the ions from the lattice, so an aqueous ionic compound can conduct.

items.stem: Explain why a solid ionic compound is a poor conductor, referring to the position of its ions.
items.modelAnswer: Solid ionic compounds are poor conductors because their ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move, so there are no mobile charged particles to carry a current.

items.stem: During the electrolysis of molten potassium bromide, a student asks whether electrons travel through the liquid. Using the particle picture of record, answer the student and name the real charge carriers.
items.modelAnswer: No: it is the ions that move and carry the charge, never electrons, when an ionic compound conducts; in the molten potassium bromide the free-moving K+ and Br- ions carry the current.

items.stem: State the aim of the electrolysis practical described in the note, naming the three solutions used.
items.modelAnswer: The aim is to electrolyse sodium chloride, dilute sulfuric acid and copper(II) sulfate solutions, collecting and identifying the products.

items.stem: State the positive test result that identifies hydrogen gas, and name the electrode at which it is collected in this practical.
items.modelAnswer: A gas that burns with a pop from a lighted splint is hydrogen, collected at the cathode.

items.stem: Explain the purpose of the inverted tubes in this practical's setup, in terms of what they capture.
items.modelAnswer: The electrodes are covered with the solution and the inverted test tubes sit over them to collect the gases that form at each electrode, so the gases can be gathered and tested.

items.stem: During the practical, one anode gas bleaches damp litmus and another anode gas relights a glowing splint. Identify each gas and state which solution produces the bleaching one.
items.modelAnswer: A gas that bleaches litmus is chlorine, and a gas that relights a glowing splint is oxygen; the chlorine comes from the sodium chloride solution, the only one of the three with a halide at the anode.

items.stem: State the two products of the electrolysis of sodium chloride solution and the electrode at which each forms.
items.modelAnswer: Sodium chloride solution splits into hydrogen gas at its cathode and chlorine gas at its anode.

items.stem: Describe the observation that shows copper has formed at the cathode in the copper(II) sulfate experiment.
items.modelAnswer: The copper appears as a pink-brown deposit on the cathode electrode.

items.stem: Explain how the litmus paper confirms which gas is emerging at the anode in the sodium chloride experiment.
items.modelAnswer: The chlorine at the anode shows itself by bleaching a piece of litmus paper, so the litmus turning white is the confirming test that the anode gas is chlorine.

items.stem: A results table is missing the row for dilute sulfuric acid. Using the pattern of record, complete the row with the product at each electrode.
items.modelAnswer: Dilute sulfuric acid splits into hydrogen gas at its cathode and oxygen gas at its anode.

items.stem: Define an electric current in terms of particles.
items.modelAnswer: An electric current is a flow of charged particles, usually electrons but sometimes ions.

items.stem: State in which physical states covalent substances can serve as insulating materials.
items.modelAnswer: Covalent substances work as insulating materials whether solid, liquid or gas.

items.stem: Explain why nothing in a covalent compound can carry a current through it.
items.modelAnswer: Covalent compounds do not conduct, since nothing charged is free to move through them and carry the current — they have no mobile charged particles.

items.stem: A salt is tested as a solid and again as a solution; only the solution lights the bulb. Using the conduction rules of record, explain both results.
items.modelAnswer: Solid ionic compounds do not conduct, because their ions are fixed in the lattice and cannot move; in solution the ionic compound conducts, because its ions can then move and carry charge.

items.stem: Define a cation and give the examples of cations named in the note.
items.modelAnswer: A cation is a positively charged ion, such as K+, Mg2+ or H+.

items.stem: State the path the electrons take through the external circuit during electrolysis.
items.modelAnswer: The electrons flow from the anode towards the cathode through the external circuit.

items.stem: Explain why cations travel to the cathode during electrolysis.
items.modelAnswer: During electrolysis, cations move towards the negatively charged electrode, the cathode; opposite charges attract, so the positive cations are drawn to the negative cathode.

items.stem: In an electrolysis cell, anions of a dye gather at one electrode. Name that electrode's charge and polarity, and state which species would gather at the other electrode.
items.modelAnswer: Anions move towards the positively charged electrode, the anode, so the dye anions gather there; the cations gather at the other electrode, the negative cathode.

items.stem: Describe what non-metal atoms do, instead of forming ions, to reach a full outer shell.
items.modelAnswer: Non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons to gain full outer shells, instead of forming ions.

items.stem: State the term for the outer electrons that take no part in a covalent bond.
items.modelAnswer: Outer electrons that take no part in the bond are called non-bonding electrons.

items.stem: Explain why a covalent bond is described as very strong.
items.modelAnswer: Each shared pair of electrons is one covalent bond, and the bonds are very strong because the shared pair grips both atoms to their full outer shells — a lot of energy is needed to break it.

items.stem: Two solids are handed to a student: one is water ice, a simple molecular substance, and one is diamond. Using the classification rule of record, sort each into its covalent structure family.
items.modelAnswer: Covalently bonded substances are either simple molecular structures, like water, or giant covalent structures, like diamond; so the ice is simple molecular and the diamond is giant covalent.

items.stem: State how a single covalent bond is drawn in a displayed formula, using hydrogen as the example.
items.modelAnswer: A covalent bond is drawn as a short straight line between the two atoms, such as H-H.

items.stem: State the charges on the shared pair and on each nucleus in a covalent bond, and what follows between them.
items.modelAnswer: The electrons in the pair carry a negative charge and each nucleus carries a positive one, so strong electrostatic attraction follows between them.

items.stem: Explain the mistake in drawing shared covalent electrons as fixed dots sitting still between two atoms.
items.modelAnswer: The shared electrons are best regarded as charge clouds in constant motion, not as points fixed in place, because the electrons move continuously within the region between the two atoms.

items.stem: A student asks why a chlorine molecule is more stable than two separate chlorine atoms. Using the noble-gas arrangement of record, answer the student.
items.modelAnswer: Sharing lets each atom reach an arrangement similar to a noble gas, which makes each atom more stable; in Cl2 each chlorine atom completes its outer shell through the shared pair.
